To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

higher levels of recreational physical activity following diagnosis of breast cancer are associated with a reduced risk of total mortality in breast cancer survivors, but are not associated with a reduced breast cancer specific or recurrence risk.

higher levels of recreational physical activity are associated with reduced risk for all-cause mortality among breast cancer survivors but are not significantly associated with risk of breast cancer mortality or recurrence.

1) physical activity was not associated with risk of breast cancer mortality and recurrence, but was associated with reduced risk for all-cause mortality, and 2) these findings were independent of other known prognostic factors, including age, tumor characteristics, and comorbidities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and evaluation of the effects of physical activity and diet in the etiology and prevention of cancer.
identifying modifiable factors that may influence the risk of breast and colon cancer.
the role of physical activity in cancer prevention and survivorship, and with the role of obesity in the development and progression of breast cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data are not sufficient at this point to support the hypothesis that physical activity is protective against breast cancer recurrence or breast cancer death.
there is insufficient evidence to support the claim that physical activity is associated with a reduced risk of recurrence or mortality from breast cancer.
physical activity does not reduce the risk of cancer recurrence, but may reduce the risk of death from all causes, and therefore, physical activity is beneficial to cancer survivors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
physical activity does not appear to be associated with breast cancer recurrence or death, but it does appear to be associated to some degree with all-cause mortality.
there is no clear evidence that physical activity is beneficial in breast cancer survivors, but there is some suggestion that it may be beneficial in terms of all-cause mortality.
physical activity after breast cancer treatment may be associated with reduced risk for all-cause mortality, but not with reduced risk of breast cancer mortality or breast cancer recurrence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
physical activity after diagnosis and treatment is associated with lower risk of all-cause mortality.
physical activity after diagnosis and treatment is associated with lower risk of death in women with early stage breast cancer.
breast cancer survivors who are physically active are less likely to die of all causes, including cancer.
